They may be either clergymen or laymen.
{{smaller block|In all cathedrals of the old foundation in England, in St. David’s, and in twelve Irish cathedrals, the ''Vicars Choral'' form a distinct corporation, the members of which vary in number from twelve to three: these corporations are distinct from the chapter as regards property, but in subjection to it as to the performance of the services.
{{right|''Grove'', Dict. Music, IV. 260.}}}}
'''Vicar forane''', in ''Rom. Cath. usage'', an ecclesiastical dignitary appointed by the bishop to exercise a limited jurisdiction in a particular town or district of his diocese. The office is analogous to that of rural dean.—'''Vicar-general''', in the ''Ch. of Eng.'', an ecclesiastical officer who assists a bishop or archbishop in the discharge of his office. The vicar-general of a bishop is his chancellor.
{{smaller block|<poem>For He that is the Formere principal

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|Viburnum|6746|vice}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|shrub of southern Europe, in Corsica forming large forests, often cultivated for its ornamental evergreen leaves, white blossoms, and dark-blue berries. ''V. Opulus'', the cranberry-tree or high cranberry, in England also known as ''white dogwood'', ''marsh-'' or ''water-elder'', and ''gaiter-tree'', is widely diffused through the north of both continents; in Norway it is used for the manufacture of small wooden articles, of spirits, and of a yellow dye. For the other European species, ''V. Lantana'', see ''wayfaring-tree''. Fourteen species occur within the United States: 11 in the northeast; the others, ''V. ellipticum'' near the Pacific, ''V. densiflorum'' and ''V. obovatum'' near the South Atlantic coast; ''V. acerifolium'' extends north to Fort Yukon, ''V. pauciflorum'' to Sitka. Two American species, ''V. Lentago'' and ''V. prunifolium'', become small trees. The bark of several species is used in the United States as a domestic remedy, and the inner bark of ''V. Lantana'' is esteemed a vesicant in England. A beverage known as Appalachian tea is sometimes made from the leaves of ''V. cassinoides'', an early-flowering, thick-leafed species of American swamps. Several species are known as ''arrow-wood'', chiefly ''V. dentatum'' in the north, ''V. molle'' in the south, ''V. ellipticum'' in California. The species are somewhat widely known by the generic name, especially ''V. acerifolium'', the maple-leafed viburnum, or dockmackie. The sweet viburnum is ''V. Lentago'' (for which see ''sheepberry''). ''V. nudum'' is known as ''withe-rod'', ''V. prunifolium'' as ''black haw'' or ''stag-bush'', and ''V. lantanoides'' as ''hobble-bush'' or ''American wayfaring-tree''. The preceding are among the most ornamental of native American shrubs, admired for their white flowers, usually compact habit, and handsome foliage, also for their fruit, a bright blue-black in ''V. prunifolium'', ''V. pubescens'', and ''V. acerifolium'', blue in ''V. dentatum'' and ''V. molle'', and bright-red in ''V. Opulus''; that of ''V. Lantana'' is an orange-red turning dull-black. Garden varieties produced by cultivation from ''V. Opulus'' are the snowball, or guelder-rose, and the rose-elder. ''V. rugosum'' of the Canaries, ''V. tomentosum'' (''V. plicatum'') of northern China, and ''V. cotinifolium'' of Nepāl, are also esteemed ornamental shrubs.}}

'''2.''' [''l. c.''] A plant of this genus.

'''vicar''' (vik′ä̤r), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''vicker''; < ME. ''vicar'', ''viker'', ''vicair'', ''vicaire'' (also ''vicary'', q. v.), < OF. (and F.) ''vicaire'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''vicario'', < L. ''vicarius'', substituted, delegated, as a noun a substitute, a deputy, vicegerent, vicar, proxy, < *''vix'' (''vic-''), found only in oblique cases (gen. ''vicis'', etc.) and pl. ''vices'', change, interchange: see ''vice''<sup>4</sup>.] '''1.''' A person deputed or authorized to perform the functions of another; a substitute in office: as, the Pope claims to be ''vicar'' of Jesus Christ on earth.
{{smaller block|He hath thee [the Virgin] maked ''vicaire'' and maistresse Of al the world.
{{right|''Chaucer'', A. B. C., l. 140.}}
Consider also the presence of the king’s majesty, God’s high ''vicar'' in earth.
{{right|''Latimer'', 6th Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}
Antichrist wee know is but the Devil’s ''Vicar.''
{{right|''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''Eng. eccles. law'', the priest of a parish the tithes of which belong to a chapter or religious house, or to a layman, and who receives only the smaller tithes or a salary. {{smaller|The title is also now given to incumbents who would formerly have been known as perpetual curates (see ''curate'').}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ye persons and ''vickers'' that haue cure and charge,
Take hede to the same, and roue not at large.</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 354.}}
All Rectors and ''Vickers'' of the same deanery (Bristol).
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 287.}}
The distinction therefore of a parson and ''vicar'' is this: the parson has for the most part the whole right to all the ecclesiastical dues in his parish; but a ''vicar'' has generally an appropriator over him, entitled to the best part of the profits, to whom he is in effect perpetual curate, with a standing salary.
{{right|''Blackstone'', Com., I. xi.}}}}
'''3.''' In the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', an ecclesiastic assisting a bishop and exercising jurisdiction in his name. He cannot perform acts properly belonging to the episcopate nor collate to benefices without special authority.—'''Cardinal vicar''', an ecclesiastical dignitary in Rome who, as delegate of the Pope, performs his functions as local bishop of the diocese of Rome.—'''Lay vicar, clerk vicar, secular vicar.''' See ''lay''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Vicar apostolic''', in ''Rom. Cath. usage'', formerly, a bishop, archbishop, or other ecclesiastic to whom the Roman pontiff delegated a portion of his jurisdiction; now, a missionary or titular bishop stationed either in a country where episcopal sees have not yet been established or in one where the succession of Roman Catholic bishops has been interrupted.—'''Vicar choral''', in the ''Ch. of Eng.'', an assistant of the canons or prebendaries in such parts of public worship as are performed in the chancel or choir, especially in connection with the music. They may be either clergymen or laymen.
{{smaller block|In all cathedrals of the old foundation in England, in St. David’s, and in twelve Irish cathedrals, the ''Vicars Choral'' form a distinct corporation, the members of which vary in number from twelve to three: these corporations are distinct from the chapter as regards property, but in subjection to it as to the performance of the services.
{{right|''Grove'', Dict. Music, IV. 260.}}}}
'''Vicar forane''', in ''Rom. Cath. usage'', an ecclesiastical dignitary appointed by the bishop to exercise a limited jurisdiction in a particular town or district of his diocese. The office is analogous to that of rural dean.—'''Vicar-general''', in the ''Ch. of Eng.'', an ecclesiastical officer who assists a bishop or archbishop in the discharge of his office. The vicar-general of a bishop is his chancellor.
{{smaller block|<poem>For He that is the Formere principal
Hath maked me [Nature] his ''vicaire-general''
To forme and peynten erthely creaturis.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Physician’s Tale, l. 20.}} Chancellors to the Bishops of Norwich exercised this power of Instituting without special powers in their patents so to do. {{right|''Rev. T. Tanner'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 331).}}}}

{{smaller block|The very first act of the new supreme Head of the Church of England was to appoint a layman as his ''Vicar-general.'' {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXVI. 829.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Vicar of (Jesus) Christ''', a title assumed by the Pope with reference to his claim to stand in the place of Jesus Christ and possess his authority in the church.—'''Vicar pensionary''', in the ''Ch. of Eng.'', a clergyman appointed at a fixed stipend to serve a church the tithes of which belong to a collegiate foundation.}}

'''vicarage''' (vik′är-āj), ''n.'' [< ''vicar'' + ''-age''.] '''1.''' The benefice of a vicar.
{{smaller block|Mr. Farebrother’s . . . was the oldest church in Middlemarch; the living, however, was but a ''vicarage'' worth barely four hundred a year. {{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xvi.}}}}
'''2.''' The house or residence of a vicar.—'''3.''' The office, position, duties, or functions of a vicar.
{{smaller block|My ''vicarage'' is to speak of his [Christ’s] compassion and his tears. {{right|''Donne'', Sermons, xiii.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Vicarage tithes.''' See ''tithe''<sup>1</sup>, 2.}}

'''vicarate''' (vik′är-āt), ''n.'' [< ''vicar'' + ''-ate''<sup>3</sup>. Cf. ''vicariate''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' The office or jurisdiction of vicar; the territory presided over by a vicar; a vicariate.—'''2.''' A number of convents united together under the supervision of a custos or vicar, but too few to constitute a province. ''Encyc. Brit.''

'''vicaress''' (vik′är-es), ''n.'' [< ''vicar'' + ''-ess''.] A female vicar; the wife of a vicar.
{{smaller block|Mother Austin was afterwards ''Vicaress'' several years. {{right|''Archæologia'', XXVIII. 198.}}}}

'''vicarial''' (vī-kā′ri-al), ''a.'' [< L. ''vicarius'', substituted, vicarious (see ''vicar'', ''vicarious''), + ''-al''.] '''1.''' Vicarious; delegated; substituted.
{{smaller block|All deriv’d and ''vicarial'' power.
{{right|''Blackwall'', Sacred Classics, II., Pref., p. xxix.}}
It has occurred to me, when weary and vexed I have myself gone to bed like a heathen, that another has asked forgiveness for my day, and safety for my night. I don’t suppose such ''vicarial'' piety will avail much.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, vii.}}}}
'''2.''' Pertaining to a vicar.
{{smaller block|The tithes of many things, as wood in particular, are in some parishes rectorial, and in some ''vicarial'', tithes.
{{right|''Blackstone'', Com., I. xi.}}}}
'''3.''' Holding the office of, or acting as, a vicar.
{{smaller block|A resident pastor, either rectorial or ''vicarial'', either an incumbent or a substitute. {{right|''V. Knox'', Sermons, VI. xxvi.}}}}

'''vicarian''' (vī-kā′ri-a̤n), ''n.'' [< LL. ''vicarianus'', of or pertaining to a deputy, < L. ''vicarius'', a deputy: see ''vicar''.] A substitute; a vicar.
{{smaller block|<poem>Shall Balbus, the demure Athenian,
Dream of the death of next ''vicarian''?</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Scourge of Villainy, iii. 134.}}}}

'''vicariate<sup>1</sup>''' (vī-kā′ri-āt), ''a.'' [< L. ''vicarius'', delegated (see ''vicar'', ''vicarious''), + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Having delegated power; pertaining to such authority and privilege as a vicar has.
{{smaller block|The ''vicariat'' authority of our see.
{{right|''Barrow'', Pope’s Supremacy, vi. § 10.}}}}

'''vicariate<sup>2</sup>''' (vī-kā′ri-āt), ''n.'' [< ML. ''vicariatus'', the office of a vicar, < L. ''vicarius'', a vicar: see ''vicar'' and ''-ate''<sup>3</sup>.] The office or authority of a vicar; office or power delegated by, or assumed in place of, another; vicarship; specifically, the jurisdiction of a vicar apostolic.
{{smaller block|That pretended spiritual dignity, . . . or, as it calleth itself, the ''vicariate'' of Christ. {{right|''Lord North''. (''Latham''.)}} The further pretensions of the Popes to the ''vicariate'' of the Empire during interregna the Germans never admitted.
{{right|''Bryce'', Holy Rom. Empire, xiii.}}}}

'''vicarii''', ''n.'' Plural of ''vicarius''.

'''vicarious''' (vī-kā′ri-us), ''a.'' [< L. ''vicarius'', that supplies the place of person or thing, substituted, delegated, vicarious: see ''vicar''.] '''1.''' Of or belonging to a vicar or substitute; deputed; delegated: as, ''vicarious'' power or authority.—'''2.''' Acting for or officially representing another: as, a ''vicarious'' agent or officer.—'''3.''' Performed or suffered for another.
{{smaller block|The ''vicarious'' work of the Great Deliverer.
{{right|''I. Taylor.''}}
All trouble and all piety are ''vicarious''. They send missionaries, at the cost of others, into foreign lands, to teach observances which they supersede at home.
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Lucian and Timotheus.}}}}
'''4.''' In ''physiol.'', substitutive: noting the performance by one organ of the functions normally belonging to another; compensatory.—{{smaller|'''Vicarious menstruation''', a discharge of blood from the nose, bowels, or other part of the body at the menstrual period, normal menstruation being absent.—'''Vicarious sacrifice''', in ''theol.'', the sacrifice of Christ on behalf and in the place of the sinner, in such a way that God accepts his suffering in lieu of the punishment which otherwise must have been inflicted on guilty man. ''L. Abbott'', Dict. Rel. Knowledge. See ''atonement'', 3.}}

'''vicariously''' (vī-kā′ri-us-li), ''adv.'' In a vicarious manner; in the place of another; by substitution or delegation. ''Burke.'' {{smaller block|chief offender but ''vicariously'' upon his agents, can come only after all the harm has been done.
{{right|''W. Wilson'', Cong. Gov., i.}}}}

'''vicariousness''' (vī-kā′ri-us-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being vicarious.
{{smaller block|Dr. Creighton puts forward another favourite assertion of the opponents of vaccination—the ''vicariousness'' of zymotic mortality.{{right|''Lancet'', 1889, II. 175.}}}}

'''vicarius''' (vī-kā′ri-us), ''n.''; pl. ''vicarii'' (-ī). [L.: see ''vicar.''] A substitute; a vicar.
{{smaller block|A new bye-law empowering the President, in his unavoidable absence, to appoint a Fellow of the College who has been a Censor to act as his ''vicarius'' was passed for the first time.{{right|''Lancet'', 1890, I. 274.}}}}

'''vicarship''' (vik′är-ship), ''n.'' [< ''vicar'' + ''-ship.''] The office or ministry of a vicar. ''Swift.''

'''vicary<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''vicary'', ''vikary'', ''vikery'', ''vicari'', < OF. ''vicaire'', etc.: see ''vicar.''] A vicar.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''vykary'' of welles, that thyder had sought
On the tenth day, that many men dyd se,
Where .iiii. yere afore he stande nor go mought,
Released he was of part of his infyrmyte.</poem>
{{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 45.}}
<poem>“Sir preest,” quod he, “artow a ''vicary'',
Or art a person? sey sooth, by my fey!”</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Parson’s Tale, l. 22.}}}}

'''vicary<sup>2</sup>''' (vik′ạ-ri), ''n.'' [< ''vicar'' + ''-y''<sup>3</sup>.] A vicarage: the quotation refers to the once common practice of the patron’s pocketing the best part of the vicar’s income.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pale Maurus paid huge simonies
For his half dozen gelded ''vicaries''.</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Scourge of Villainy, v. 65.}}}}

'''vice<sup>1</sup>''' (vīs), ''n.'' [< ME. ''vice'', ''vyce'', < OF. ''vice'', F. ''vice'' = Sp. Pg. ''vicio'' = It. ''vizio'', < L. ''vitium'', ML. also ''vicium'', a vice, fault; root uncertain. Hence ult. ''vicious'', ''vitiate''.] '''1.''' Fault; mistake; error: as, a ''vice'' of method.
{{smaller block|He with a manly voys seith his message, . . .
Withouten ''vice'' of sillable or of lettre.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire’s Tale, l. 93.}}}}
'''2.''' An imperfection; a defect; a blemish: as, a ''vice'' of conformation; a ''vice'' of literary style.
{{smaller block|<poem>Myda hadde under his longe heres,
Growynge upon his heed, two asses eres,
The which ''vice'' he hidde as he best myghte.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 99.}}
Euen so parsimonie and illiberâlitie are greater ''vices'' in a Prince than in a priuate person.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 34.}}
To be wanting therefore in those principal affections which respect the good of the whole constitution must be a ''vice'' and imperfection. ''Shaftesbury'', Inquiry, II. i. § 3.
Ferocity and insolence were not among the ''vices'' of the national character. ''Macaulay'', Machiavelli.}}
'''3.''' Any immoral or evil habit or practice; evil conduct in which a person indulges; a particular form of wickedness or depravity; immorality; specifically, the indulgence of impure or degrading appetites or passions: as, the ''vice'' of drunkenness; hence, also, a fault or bad trick in a lower animal, as a horse.
{{smaller block|This Baron was right wise, and full of euell ''vyces''.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 51.}}
Lord, Lord, how subject we old men are to this ''vice'' of lying! ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 2. 325.
When ''vices'' become so notorious that they are a reproach and a by-word to Neighbour Nations.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, II. iv.}}
''Vices'' so splendid and alluring as to resemble virtues.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.}}}}

{{smaller block|Him as had no ''wice'', and was so free from temper that a infant might ha’ drove him.
{{right|''Dickens'', Master Humphrey’s Clock, Conclusion.}}}}
{{smaller block|Reared under an open shed, and early habituated to the sight of men, to the sound and glitter of weapons, and to all the accessories of human life, the colt grows up free from ''vice'' or timidity.
{{right|''W. G. Palgrave.''}}}}
'''4.''' Depravity; corruption of morals or manners: in a collective sense and without a plural: as, an age of ''vice''.
{{smaller block|Be dilligent for to detecte a seruaunt gyven to ''vyce.''
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 84.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Vice'' is the foulest Prison, and in this
Not John, but Herod the close Pris’ner is.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, iii. 167.}}}}
{{smaller block|Virtue is the Good and ''Vice'' the Ill of every one.
{{right|''Shaftesbury'', Inquiry, II. ii. § 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When ''vice'' prevails, and impious men bear sway,
The post of honour is a private station.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Civilisation has on the whole been more successful in repressing crime than in repressing ''vice.''
{{right|''Lecky'', Europ. Morals, I. 157.}}}}
'''5.''' Depravity or corruption of the physical organization; some morbid state of the system: as, he inherited a constitutional ''vice'' which resulted in consumption.—'''6.''' Viciousness; ugliness; mischievousness.
{{smaller block|Half the ''vice'' of the Slogger’s hitting is neutralized, for he daren’t lunge out freely for fear of exposing his sides.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 5.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
